lexemes.note: An existential particle (Wiktionary files it as an adverb). Possession: יֵשׁ + לְ + possessor (יֵשׁ לִי); its negation is אֵין.

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s second sense is “someone/something has” (with לְ) — exactly this concept; the check only misses it because the gloss is worded with “has”.

profile.feeling: Hebrew “has” nothing — things “are there for” you: יֵשׁ לִי.

senses.def: with לְ: to have (possession) — יֵשׁ לִי “I have”

examples.tr: Is there milk in the fridge?

phrases.meaning: maybe; it’s possible; is there a chance?

synonyms.nuance: inflected form “he/it is there, exists” (יֶשְׁנוֹ, יֶשְׁנָהּ …), used in formal writing

antonyms.note: there isn’t; (with לְ) not to have

etymology.text: Related to Aramaic אִית (ʾīṯ). Compare Arabic لَيْسَ (laysa, “to not be, there is not”).

funFacts: Wiktionary compares Arabic لَيْسَ (laysa, “is not”), which is often explained as “not” + this same existential word.
pitfalls: יֵשׁ never changes for person: יֵשׁ לִי, יֵשׁ לוֹ, יֵשׁ לָנוּ — the owner is shown by לְ with a suffix.
The negative is אֵין, never *לֹא יֵשׁ: אֵין לִי גֶּזֶר.
Only present: “I had” = הָיָה לִי / הָיְתָה לִי, “I will have” = יִהְיֶה לִי.
subtleties: The thing possessed is grammatically the subject, so standard Hebrew puts no אֶת before it (יֵשׁ לִי הַסֵּפֶר); colloquially יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר is very common.

lexemes.role: “to, for”: the prefix written onto the next word (לְאִמָּא “to / for Mum”), fused with the article as לַ (לַשּׁוּק “to the market”) or לָ before הָ (לָעֲבוֹדָה, לָאוֹטוֹבּוּס); before a shva it is לִ (לִשְׂדֵה הַתְּעוּפָה). With יֵשׁ / אֵין it marks the possessor (יֵשׁ לִי “I have”). With a pronoun it takes endings and is written as a word of its own (לִי, לְךָ, לוֹ …).

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s glosses of the prefix ל־ (“to; for; …”) do not contain the words of the course gloss “to (towards a place)”; לְ is the standard “to” of Modern Hebrew (לַשּׁוּק “to the market”).

override.N;SG;DEF;PFX: the definite form after the fused prepositions בַּ / לַ / לָ (בְּ / לְ + the article), which drop the ה of the article: הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה → (בַּ / לַ)מִּשְׁפָּחָה; Wiktionary lists only the full definite form הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה.

profile.feeling: Home, warmth and duties — the family is the centre of Israeli life (Friday-night dinners, holidays together).

senses.def: family (in biology: a rank of classification)

examples.tr: The cat and the lion are from the same family.

synonyms.nuance: “home, household” — הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי can mean the people at home, my family
“tribe” — said jokingly of a very large family

etymology.text: Wiktionary: perhaps related to שִׁפְחָה (shifkhá) “female slave, maidservant” — the people of one household.

funFacts: The suffixed forms show the old -at- ending that the plain word hides: מִשְׁפָּחָה → מִשְׁפַּחַת־ → מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי “my family”.
In biology it is exactly English family: the rank just above the genus (סוּג).
pitfalls: “My family” in everyday speech is הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁלִּי; מִשְׁפַּחְתִּי is formal or written.
The article is needed before שֶׁלִּי: הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁלָּנוּ “our family”; מִשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁלָּנוּ would be “a family of ours”.
subtleties: כָּל הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה is “the whole family”: with a definite singular noun כָּל means “whole”, not “every”.

lexemes.note: Used in the plural; the singular הוֹרֶה “a parent” is formal.

profile.feeling: Mum and Dad together — the word of school forms and of daily talk alike.

examples.text: מָחָר יֵשׁ אֲסֵפַת הוֹרִים בְּבֵית הַסֵּפֶר.
examples.tr: Tomorrow there is a parents’ meeting at school.

collocations.tr: the parents’ home (where one grew up)

phrases.tr: honour your father and your mother
phrases.meaning: the commandment to respect one’s parents

synonyms.nuance: “Mum and Dad” — how people speak of their own parents at home

etymology.text: The plural of הוֹרֶה “parent” (Wiktionary); Wiktionary also lists a rare feminine הוֹרָה “mother”.

funFacts: Do not confuse it with הוֹרָה, the Israeli circle dance: that word came through Yiddish from Greek χορός “dance” (English chorus).
pitfalls: There is no everyday singular: the formal הוֹרֶה “a parent” appears in official language; “one of my parents” is אֶחָד הַהוֹרִים שֶׁלִּי.
It is masculine plural: הַהוֹרִים הָאֵלֶּה, הֵם.
subtleties: The suffixed הוֹרַי “my parents” sounds a little formal; in conversation הַהוֹרִים שֶׁלִּי is usual.

lexemes.note: Used like a name: אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי “my mum” (no article); calling her: אִמָּא!

profile.feeling: Mum — warm and everyday; adults say it too.

senses.def: Mum! (calling one’s mother; used like a name, without the article)

phrases.meaning: oh no! oh my God! — a cry of fright or surprise

synonyms.nuance: the formal and written word (forms, the news, literature), also figurative: “mother of …”

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic אִמָּא (ʾimmā); the inherited Hebrew word is אֵם (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The final -ָא of אִמָּא, אַבָּא and סָבְתָא is the Aramaic “emphatic” (definite) ending — and Hebrew indeed uses these words like names, without הַ.
pitfalls: With שֶׁלִּי it usually goes without the article, like a name: אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי (הָאִמָּא שֶׁלִּי is also heard in speech).
No suffix on this word: “my mum” is אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי, or the formal אִמִּי (from אֵם).
subtleties: Children and adults alike say אִמָּא; a sentence with אִמִּי sounds like a speech or a book.

profile.feeling: Mother in the formal sense — documents, the news, literature and figures of speech.

senses.def: mother, origin (figurative: “the mother of …”, שְׂפַת אֵם “mother tongue”)

phrases.text: שְׁמַע בְּנִי מוּסַר אָבִיךָ וְאַל תִּטֹּשׁ תּוֹרַת אִמֶּךָ
phrases.tr: hear, my son, your father’s instruction, and do not forsake your mother’s teaching
phrases.meaning: listen to what your parents teach you

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word, used like a name: אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔimm- (Wiktionary). Cognate with Arabic أُمّ (ʔumm).

funFacts: Arabic أُمّ (umm) is the same word — as in names like أُمّ كُلْثُوم (Umm Kulthum), “mother of Kulthum”.
pitfalls: With a suffix the vowel changes and the מ doubles: אִמִּי, אִמּוֹ, אִמָּהּ.
Do not confuse it with אִם “if”: the same letters, other vowels.
subtleties: In speech אִמִּי sounds formal or solemn (a speech at a wedding, a memorial); everyday “my mother” is אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי.

lexemes.note: Used like a name: אַבָּא שֶׁלִּי “my dad” (no article); calling him: אַבָּא!

profile.feeling: Dad — warm and everyday.

senses.def: Dad! (calling one’s father; used like a name, without the article)

synonyms.nuance: the formal and written word (forms, the news, literature), also “founder, forefather”

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic אַבָּא (ʾabbā), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *ʾab-; a doublet of the inherited אָב (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Through the Aramaic of the Gospels (“Abba, Father”) the word reached Greek ἀββᾶς and Latin abbas — the source of English abbot and German Abt.
pitfalls: Like אִמָּא it goes without the article before שֶׁלִּי: אַבָּא שֶׁלִּי.
The standard plural is אָבוֹת, the plural of אָב.
subtleties: Stress the first syllable: ÁBA.

profile.feeling: Father as a role and an origin — formal and solemn; also founder and forefather.

examples.tr: The father and the son were there.
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are the Patriarchs.

phrases.meaning: the opening words of a prayer of the High Holidays

phrases.text: אָבוֹת אָכְלוּ בֹסֶר וְשִׁנֵּי בָנִים תִּקְהֶינָה
phrases.tr: the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge
phrases.meaning: children suffer for what their parents did

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word, used like a name: אַבָּא שֶׁלִּי

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔabw-; cognate with Arabic أَب (ʔab). A doublet of אַבָּא, which was borrowed from Aramaic (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Many names begin with it: אַבְרָהָם, אַבְנֵר, אֲבִישָׁלוֹם (Absalom, “my father is peace”).
Arabic أَبُو (abū) “father of” in names (Abu Bakr) is the same word.
pitfalls: With suffixes it adds -ִי-: אָבִי “my father”, אָבִיו “his father”, אָבִיהָ “her father” — like אָח.
The plural אָבוֹת ends in -וֹת although the word is masculine.
subtleties: Before another noun it is אֲבִי־ “father of”: אֲבִי הַכַּלָּה “the bride’s father”.

lexemes.note: Construct form בֶּן “son of; aged” (בֶּן דּוֹד, בֶּן שֵׁשׁ).

profile.feeling: A son — and a whole family of expressions: “son of” means belonging, age and membership.

senses.def: (בֶּן + number) aged: הוּא בֶּן שֵׁשׁ “he is six”
(בֶּן + noun) one who belongs to: בֶּן אָדָם “person”, בֶּן זוּג “partner”

examples.tr: We have a son and a daughter.

phrases.tr: a wise son makes a father glad
phrases.meaning: good children are their parents’ joy

synonyms.nuance: “child, boy” — הַיֶּלֶד שֶׁלִּי “my kid” is the everyday way to speak of a young son

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *bin-; the old vowel survives in names such as בִּנְיָמִין (Benjamin) and יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן־נוּן “Joshua son of Nun” (Wiktionary). Cognate with Arabic اِبْن (ibn).

funFacts: Arabic اِبْن (ibn) / bin is the same word: Hebrew בֶּן־ and Arabic bin both mean “son of” in names.
pitfalls: Before another noun it becomes בֶּן: בֶּן דּוֹד, בֶּן שֵׁשׁ — and the plural בָּנִים becomes בְּנֵי: בְּנֵי דּוֹדִים.
בָּנִים also means simply “boys” (בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת “boys and girls”); “children” in general is יְלָדִים.
subtleties: Age in years is said with בֶּן / בַּת and a feminine number, because שָׁנִים “years” is feminine: הוּא בֶּן שָׁלוֹשׁ “he is three” (but בֶּן שְׁלוֹשָׁה חֳדָשִׁים “three months old”).

profile.feeling: A daughter — and, as with בֵּן, “daughter of” for age and belonging.

senses.def: (בַּת + number) aged (of a woman or a girl): הִיא בַּת שֵׁשׁ

phrases.meaning: a voice from heaven; a faint echo

synonyms.nuance: “girl, child” — הַיַּלְדָּה שֶׁלִּי “my little girl” is the everyday way to speak of a young daughter

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bint-: the i became a (Philippi’s law) and the n assimilated to the t. Cognate with Arabic بِنْت (bint) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: בַּת יָם, a city south of Tel Aviv, is literally “daughter of the sea”.
Arabic بِنْت (bint) keeps the n that Hebrew בַּת lost — but Hebrew shows it again in the plural בָּנוֹת.
pitfalls: The plural is בָּנוֹת — the n of *bint- comes back — not *בַּתּוֹת.
With suffixes the vowel becomes i and the ת doubles: בִּתִּי “my daughter”, בִּתּוֹ “his daughter”.
subtleties: הַבָּנוֹת often means just “the girls (of the group)”.

profile.feeling: A brother — and, as אָחִי, the Israeli “bro”.

senses.def: brother; (plural אַחִים) brothers, or brothers and sisters
brother, fellow; אָחִי “bro, mate” as a friendly address

examples.tr: I have a brother and a sister.
He is a nurse in a hospital.
The nurse is coming to check on you.

phrases.text: הִנֵּה מַה טּוֹב וּמַה נָּעִים שֶׁבֶת אַחִים גַּם יָחַד
phrases.tr: how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to sit together
phrases.meaning: the joy of unity and friendship (a well-known song)

synonyms.nuance: for the second sense: a female nurse, and the usual name of the profession

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔaḫw- (Wiktionary). Cognate with Arabic أَخ (ʔax).

funFacts: Arabic أَخ (akh) is the same word, and أَخِي (akhī) “my brother” is a friendly address there too — like Israeli אָחִי.
pitfalls: The plural has a patah: אָח → אַחִים, הָאַחִים.
With suffixes it adds -ִי-: אָחִיו “his brother”, אָחִיהָ “her brother” (like אָב).
אַחִים also means “siblings” for a mixed group: כַּמָּה אַחִים יֵשׁ לְךָ? “how many brothers and sisters do you have?”
subtleties: אָחִי is both “my brother” and the slang “bro” between friends; only the context tells.

profile.feeling: A sister — and the nurse at the hospital.

senses.def: nurse (a woman; also the profession in general)

examples.tr: She is a nurse in a hospital.
The nurses work at night too.

phrases.tr: you have captured my heart, my sister, my bride

synonyms.nuance: for the second sense: a male nurse

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔaḫwat- (Wiktionary). Cognate with Arabic أُخْت (ʔuxt).

funFacts: A nurse is a “sister” in Hebrew as in British English (Sister), in German (Krankenschwester) and in Russian (медсестра, from медицинская сестра “medical sister”).
pitfalls: The plural is irregular: אֲחָיוֹת, הָאֲחָיוֹת (not *אָחוֹתוֹת).
With suffixes the first vowel shortens: אֲחוֹתִי “my sister”, אֲחוֹתוֹ “his sister”.
subtleties: A male nurse is אָח, a female nurse אָחוֹת — the same pair as brother and sister.

profile.feeling: The usual word for “husband” — though at heart it means “owner”, which makes some couples avoid it.

senses.def: (בַּעַל + noun) having, endowed with: בַּעַל נִסָּיוֹן “experienced”

examples.tr: The owner of the flat lives upstairs.

collocations.tr: the landlord; the master of the house

phrases.text: תִּקְרְאִי אִישִׁי וְלֹא תִקְרְאִי לִי עוֹד בַּעְלִי
phrases.tr: you will call me “my man”, and no longer call me “my master”
phrases.meaning: a relationship of love, not of ownership — quoted in the modern debate about the word

synonyms.nuance: “partner, spouse” — neutral and equal; preferred by many couples and in official language
“man” — אִישִׁי “my husband” is the Biblical alternative (Hosea 2:18), chosen today by some who reject בַּעַל

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *baʕl- “owner, lord”; the same word is the name of the Canaanite god Baal (Wiktionary). Cognate with Arabic بَعْل (baʿl) “husband”.

funFacts: The Canaanite storm god Baal is simply “the Lord, the Owner” — the same word.
Arabic بَعْل (baʿl) also means “husband” (Qur’an 11:72), though everyday Arabic says زَوْج (zawj).
pitfalls: בַּעַל literally means “owner, master”; many couples avoid it for that reason and say בֶּן הַזּוּג שֶׁלִּי “my partner”.
The plural בְּעָלִים is usually heard as “owners” (הַבְּעָלִים שֶׁל הַדִּירָה).
subtleties: In the suffixed forms the guttural ע takes a hataf: בַּעֲלִי, בַּעֲלָהּ.

profile.feeling: A baby — small, soft and loud; the default word for any baby.

senses.def: baby, infant (a baby boy, or any baby)

examples.tr: There are ten babies at the nursery.

phrases.tr: a baby who was taken captive
phrases.meaning: someone who never learned the tradition, through no fault of his own

synonyms.nuance: a toddler, a small child (about one to three) — official and educational language
an infant, a babe — poetic and Biblical

etymology.text: Wiktionary links it to יָנַק “to suckle” and יַנְקוּת “infancy”.

funFacts: Its relative יָנַק “to suckle” also gives יוֹנֵק “mammal” — literally “one that suckles”.
pitfalls: The plural is תִּינוֹקוֹת although the word is masculine: עֲשָׂרָה תִּינוֹקוֹת (masculine number).
A baby girl is תִּינֹקֶת; for any baby, or when the sex does not matter, say תִּינוֹק.
subtleties: Israelis give a baby’s age with בֶּן / בַּת: תִּינוֹק בֶּן חֹדֶשׁ “a month-old baby”.

profile.feeling: A baby girl.

synonyms.nuance: any baby — also a girl, when her sex is not the point

etymology.text: The feminine of תִּינוֹק “baby” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The pair תִּינוֹק / תִּינֹקֶת works like יֶלֶד / יַלְדָּה: Hebrew names the sex even of a newborn.
pitfalls: The plural תִּינוֹקוֹת is the same as that of תִּינוֹק; only agreement shows the gender: שָׁלוֹשׁ תִּינוֹקוֹת (girls), שְׁלוֹשָׁה תִּינוֹקוֹת (boys or a mix).
subtleties: In full spelling it is written תינוקת, with a ו, although the vowel sign is a short holam (תִּינֹקֶת).

lexemes.note: The plural of סָב “grandfather”, used for “grandparents”.

profile.feeling: Grandparents as a group — the word of schools, speeches and adverts; at home people say סַבָּא וְסָבְתָא.

examples.tr: The grandparents are coming on Saturday.
Grandfathers and grandmothers are a big help.

synonyms.nuance: “Grandpa and Grandma” — how people speak of their own grandparents

etymology.text: The plural of סָב “grandfather, old man”, from Aramaic סָבָא “elder, grandfather” (Wiktionary, סָב).

funFacts: Like Greek οι παππούδες, Hebrew uses the plural of “grandfather” for “grandparents”; German has a word of its own, Großeltern.
pitfalls: It is a masculine plural used for a mixed group: הַסָּבִים = the grandparents (or only the grandfathers).
subtleties: At home: סַבָּא וְסָבְתָא שֶׁלִּי; in writing or in a speech: הַסָּבִים שֶׁלִּי.

lexemes.note: Used like a name (סַבָּא שֶׁלִּי). Its plural is not used: “grandfathers, grandparents” is סָבִים.

profile.feeling: Grandpa — affectionate, used like a name.

senses.def: Grandpa! (calling or naming one’s grandfather, without the article)

synonyms.nuance: the formal and written word; סָבִי “my grandfather”

etymology.text: From Aramaic סָבָא (sāḇā) “elder, grandfather” (Wiktionary, under סָב).

funFacts: סַבָּא רַבָּא “great-grandfather” and סָבְתָא רַבְּתָא “great-grandmother” are pure Aramaic: “great grandfather”.
pitfalls: Say SÁ-ba with b: the ב has a dagesh (סַבָּא) — but סָבְתָא is SÁV-ta, with v.
It is hardly ever made plural; “grandfathers, grandparents” is סָבִים.
subtleties: Like אִמָּא it is used as a name, without the article: סַבָּא בַּבַּיִת “Grandpa is at home”.

profile.feeling: Grandfather in formal language; also an old, wise man.

examples.tr: The grandfather and the grandson were there.
She has a grandfather and a grandmother.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word, used like a name: סַבָּא שֶׁלִּי
“an old man” — for the second sense

etymology.text: From Aramaic סָבָא (sāḇā) “ancestor; elder; grandfather”; related to native Hebrew שָׂב (sav) “grey-haired, old” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its native Hebrew cousin שֵׂיבָה means “grey hair, old age”.
pitfalls: It is formal: הַסָּב שֶׁלִּי sounds stiff at home — say סַבָּא שֶׁלִּי.
subtleties: סָבִי “my grandfather” is the usual form in writing (dedications, biographies).

profile.feeling: Grandma — soup, stories and spoiling.

senses.def: Grandma! (calling or naming one’s grandmother, without the article)

examples.tr: The grandmothers are sitting in the garden.

synonyms.nuance: the formal and written word; סָבָתִי “my grandmother”

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic סָבְתָא (Wiktionary).

funFacts: שַׂעֲרוֹת סָבְתָא, “grandma’s hair”, is the Hebrew name of candy floss (cotton candy).
pitfalls: No dagesh in the ב: SÁV-ta (but סַבָּא is SÁ-ba).
The plural is סָבְתוֹת.
subtleties: Like אִמָּא it is used as a name: סָבְתָא אוֹמֶרֶת … “Grandma says …”.

profile.feeling: Grandmother in formal language.

examples.tr: She has a grandfather and a grandmother.
The grandmother and the granddaughter went for a walk.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word, used like a name: סָבְתָא שֶׁלִּי

etymology.text: The feminine of סָב “grandfather” (Wiktionary lists the pair); Wiktionary marks סָבָה as formal.

funFacts: Formal סָב / סָבָה and everyday סַבָּא / סָבְתָא mirror אָב / אֵם and אַבָּא / אִמָּא: Hebrew keeps two registers for the closest family.
pitfalls: Do not confuse it with סִבָּה “reason, cause” (other vowels; in full spelling סיבה).
subtleties: With suffixes the old -at- appears: סָבָתִי “my grandmother”, סָבָתוֹ “his grandmother”.

profile.feeling: A grandson — the pride of every grandmother.

examples.tr: They have a grandson and a granddaughter.

profile.synonymsNone: No other word for a grandson; a great-grandchild is נִין.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology. The word is old: the Bible pairs it with נִין in נִין וָנֶכֶד “offspring and posterity” (Isaiah 14:22).

funFacts: Grandparents and grandchildren come as a pair in Hebrew too: סָבִים וּנְכָדִים.
pitfalls: The plural נְכָדִים covers grandchildren of both sexes.
The first vowel drops in the plural: נֶכֶד → נְכָדִים.
subtleties: In the Bible נֶכֶד means “posterity, offspring” in general (נִין וָנֶכֶד); the exact meaning “grandson” is modern.

profile.feeling: A granddaughter.
profile.synonymsNone: No other word for a granddaughter.

etymology.text: The feminine of נֶכֶד “grandson” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: נֶכֶד / נֶכְדָּה follow the most common pattern of Hebrew pairs: the feminine adds -ָה.
pitfalls: נְכָדוֹת is only for granddaughters; a mixed group is נְכָדִים.
subtleties: With suffixes (formal): נֶכְדָּתִי “my granddaughter”.

profile.feeling: An uncle, on either side of the family — and, for children, any grown-up family friend.

senses.def: uncle (a brother of one’s father or mother, or an aunt’s husband)

examples.tr: My beloved is mine and I am his.

phrases.meaning: a rich benefactor who will solve all your problems

phrases.tr: my beloved is mine and I am his

profile.synonymsNone: One word for both sides of the family; Hebrew has no separate word for the father’s or the mother’s brother.

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic *dād- “paternal uncle”; in Biblical Hebrew it also means “beloved” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic separates the father’s brother عَمّ (ʿamm) from the mother’s brother خَال (khāl), and Turkish too (amca / dayı); Hebrew דּוֹד covers both, like German Onkel, Greek θείος and Russian дядя.
The name דָּוִד (David) is traditionally explained as “beloved”, from the same root.
pitfalls: Do not confuse it with דּוּד (dud) “water boiler” — one vowel apart, and Israelis talk about the דּוּד every winter.
The plural דּוֹדִים can mean uncles, or uncles and aunts together.
subtleties: Children call a grown-up man close to the family דּוֹד, and a woman דּוֹדָה — like German Onkel and Tante.

profile.feeling: An aunt, on either side of the family.

senses.def: aunt (a sister of one’s father or mother, or an uncle’s wife)

profile.synonymsNone: One word for the father’s and the mother’s sister (Arabic عَمَّة / خَالَة, Turkish hala / teyze).

etymology.text: דּוֹד “uncle” + the feminine ending ־ָה (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish needs three words where Hebrew has דּוֹדָה: hala (father’s sister), teyze (mother’s sister) and yenge (an uncle’s wife).
pitfalls: The plural is דּוֹדוֹת; a mixed group of uncles and aunts is דּוֹדִים.
subtleties: דּוֹדָה is also an uncle’s wife: Hebrew does not separate aunts by blood from aunts by marriage.

override.N;PL;INDF: Wiktionary writes the plural with a maqaf (בְּנֵי־דוֹדִים / בְּנֵי־דוֹד); the course writes this multi-word noun with a space, like its lemma בֶּן דּוֹד, so the two spellings differ only in the hyphen (and the dagesh it removes).

profile.feeling: A cousin — close family in Israel; in slang also an ironic name for Arabs (“cousins” through Abraham).

senses.def: an Arab (slang, from the shared descent from Abraham; can sound patronizing)

examples.tr: The cousins are coming to the wedding.

synonyms.nuance: a cousin through an aunt (the son of one’s aunt)

etymology.text: A compound: בֶּן “son of” + דּוֹד “uncle” — “the uncle’s son” (Wiktionary, בֶּן־דּוֹד).

funFacts: Arabic paints the same picture: اِبْن عَمّ (ibn ʿamm) “son of the (paternal) uncle” is a cousin.
pitfalls: The definite form puts הַ on the second word: בֶּן הַדּוֹד “the cousin” (in speech also הַבֶּן דּוֹד).
The plural changes the first word: בְּנֵי דּוֹדִים (or בְּנֵי דּוֹד).
In slang בְּנֵי דּוֹדִים can mean “Arabs” — it can sound patronizing.
subtleties: Strictly it is the son of an uncle; for an aunt’s son one can say בֶּן דּוֹדָה, but בֶּן דּוֹד serves for every male cousin.

override.N;PL;INDF: Wiktionary writes the plural with a maqaf (בְּנוֹת־דּוֹדִים / בְּנוֹת־דּוֹד); the course writes this multi-word noun with a space, like its lemma בַּת דּוֹד.

profile.feeling: A female cousin.

synonyms.nuance: a cousin through an aunt (the daughter of one’s aunt) — very common in speech

etymology.text: A compound: בַּת “daughter of” + דּוֹד “uncle” (Wiktionary, בַּת־דּוֹד).

funFacts: Esther was Mordecai’s cousin: the Bible calls her בַּת־דֹּדוֹ, “the daughter of his uncle” (Esther 2:7).
pitfalls: The plural is בְּנוֹת דּוֹדִים (or בְּנוֹת דּוֹד); a mixed group of cousins is בְּנֵי דּוֹדִים.
The definite form: בַּת הַדּוֹד “the cousin”.
subtleties: Many speakers choose by the parent: בַּת דּוֹד (an uncle’s daughter), בַּת דּוֹדָה (an aunt’s daughter).

profile.feeling: A nephew.

examples.text: יֵשׁ לוֹ שְׁלוֹשָׁה אַחִים וְשִׁבְעָה אַחְיָנִים.
examples.tr: He has three brothers and seven nephews and nieces.

profile.synonymsNone: No other everyday word; older Hebrew said בֶּן אָח “a brother’s son”.

etymology.text: Built on אָח “brother”: the child of one’s brother or sister. Wiktionary gives no further etymology.

funFacts: Hebrew builds “nephew” from “brother” (אָח → אַחְיָן), as Arabic says اِبْن أَخ (ibn akh) “son of a brother”.
pitfalls: In full spelling it has two yods: אחיין.
A mixed group is אַחְיָנִים.
subtleties: The word covers the son of a brother and of a sister alike.

profile.feeling: A niece.
profile.synonymsNone: No other everyday word for a niece.

etymology.text: The feminine of אַחְיָן “nephew” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The ending -ִית makes feminines of many nouns: סְטוּדֶנְט / סְטוּדֶנְטִית, אַחְיָן / אַחְיָנִית.
pitfalls: The plural ends in -יּוֹת: אַחְיָנִיּוֹת (like סְטוּדֶנְטִית → סְטוּדֶנְטִיּוֹת).
subtleties: In speech one also hears אַחְיָנִית שֶׁלִּי without הַ: “a niece of mine”.

profile.feeling: Any relative — the wide circle of a family.

senses.def: a relative, a family member (a man, or anyone)

examples.tr: He is a relative of mine.

examples.text: בַּחַג בָּאִים אֵלֵינוּ קְרוֹבֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה מִכָּל הָאָרֶץ.
examples.tr: On the holiday relatives come to us from all over the country.

synonyms.nuance: the short form: הוּא קָרוֹב שֶׁלִּי; plural קְרוֹבִים “relatives”
“a family member” — someone who belongs to the family, or is treated as if he did

etymology.text: קָרוֹב “near, close” (in its construct form קְרוֹב־) + מִשְׁפָּחָה “family”: “one near in the family”. Wiktionary gives קָרוֹב “a relative” and notes the same root as Arabic قَرِيب (qarīb) “near”.

funFacts: Arabic قَرِيب (qarīb) also means both “near” and “relative”; Turkish took the Arabic plural as akraba “relatives”.
pitfalls: Only the first word changes: קְרוֹבֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה; the article goes on the second word: קְרוֹב הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה.
subtleties: With שֶׁלִּי and no article it means “a relative of mine”: הוּא קְרוֹב מִשְׁפָּחָה שֶׁלִּי.

profile.feeling: A female relative.

examples.tr: She is a relative of ours.
A relative of mine works here.

synonyms.nuance: the short form: הִיא קְרוֹבָה שֶׁלִּי

etymology.text: קְרוֹבָה “a female relative” (Wiktionary) in its construct form קְרוֹבַת־ + מִשְׁפָּחָה “family”.

funFacts: The -ַת of קְרוֹבַת is the old feminine ending that every -ָה noun shows before another noun: מִשְׁפָּחָה → מִשְׁפַּחַת, קְרוֹבָה → קְרוֹבַת.
pitfalls: The first word ends in -ַת: קְרוֹבַת מִשְׁפָּחָה, not *קְרוֹבָה מִשְׁפָּחָה.
subtleties: A group of men and women together is קְרוֹבֵי מִשְׁפָּחָה.

lexemes.note: שֶׁל + “me”: after a definite noun, הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי “my house”. The same for a man and a woman speaking.
שֶׁל + “you” (to a man): הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלְּךָ “your book”. To a woman: שֶׁלָּךְ.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses it grammatically, as “form of שֶׁל including the second-person masculine singular personal pronoun” — which is exactly “your”; the check looks for the English word “your”, which that gloss does not contain.

lexemes.note: שֶׁל + “you” (to a woman): הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלָּךְ “your book”. To a man: שֶׁלְּךָ.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses it grammatically, as “form of שֶׁל including the second-person feminine singular personal pronoun” — which is exactly “your”; the check looks for the English word “your”, which that gloss does not contain.

lexemes.note: שֶׁל + “him”: הַבַּיִת שֶׁלּוֹ “his house”. It follows the owner, not the thing.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses it grammatically, as “form of שֶׁל including the third-person masculine singular personal pronoun” — which is exactly “his”; the check looks for the English word “his”, which that gloss does not contain.

lexemes.note: שֶׁל + “her”: הַבַּיִת שֶׁלָּהּ “her house”. The final ה is pronounced h in careful speech (shelah).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses it grammatically, as “form of שֶׁל including the third-person feminine singular personal pronoun” — which is exactly “her”; the check looks for the English word “her”, which that gloss does not contain.

Wiktionary glosses it grammatically, as “form of שֶׁל including the first-person plural personal pronoun” — which is exactly “our”; the check looks for the English word “our”, which that gloss does not contain.

lexemes.note: שֶׁל + “you” (several people, men or a mixed group): הַבַּיִת שֶׁלָּכֶם. To women only: שֶׁלָּכֶן.
שֶׁל + “you” (several women): הַבַּיִת שֶׁלָּכֶן. In casual speech many use שֶׁלָּכֶם for women too.
שֶׁל + “them” (men or a mixed group): הַבַּיִת שֶׁלָּהֶם. Women only: שֶׁלָּהֶן.
שֶׁל + “them” (women only): הַבַּיִת שֶׁלָּהֶן. In casual speech many use שֶׁלָּהֶם for women too.

lexemes.role: “of” (belonging): הַתִּיק שֶׁל דָּנָה “Dana’s bag”. With a pronoun it fuses into one word: שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁלְּךָ, שֶׁלָּךְ, שֶׁלּוֹ … (my, your, his …).
